entries.title: Astronomers Have Completed the Largest Map of Space. Yes, You Can Play With It.
entries.summary: The intricate, 5.6 trillion-pixel map covers approximately 75 percent of the sky and includes about 4 billion celestial objects.
entries.content:
The driving force behind our universe’s accelerated expansion remains one of the greatest mysteries in astronomy. While this force, which scientists refer to as dark energy, pervades our universe, we know almost nothing about it.

Located on a remote mountain in Arizona’s Sonoran Desert, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) has spent the past five years mapping the cosmos with the goal of unraveling this mystery. The result is the largest three-dimensional map of the universe ever created. And now—with the release of the latest version of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, a free online tool for exploring the vast imaging data—you too can poke around the universe.

The new map boasts an overwhelming amount of information: 5.6 trillion pixels containing approximately 4 billion celestial objects including stars, galaxies, black holes, and asteroids. It covers approximately 75 percent of the entire sky, recording both visible light and near-infrared wavelengths.

Those missing pieces include the deeper parts of space blocked by the stars, space dust, and other matter in our own galaxy, which is a major challenge for astronomy surveys, especially ground-based ones. However, since the Milky Way is splayed out like a fried egg—which is why it appears as a dense band of stars in the night sky—the researchers aim DESI’s 5,000 mechanical eyes out of the top or bottom of our galaxy to capture some of the clearest images of distant space yet.

Though this particular survey lasted five years, it built on another 13 years of groundwork. More than 160 scientists were involved in data collection, and over the course of the project, researchers have already published upwards of 1,800 scientific papers referencing the data.

“It’s part of the fabric of astronomy research now,” David Schlegel, a researcher at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and co-lead of the Legacy Surveys, said in a press release. “When you're working with astronomical objects today, you often start by pulling up the Legacy Imaging Viewer to see what you’re looking at.”

Earlier this year, DESI researchers released another map, which projected the distances of 47 million galaxies and quasars. This reconstructed 11 billion years of cosmic history, bringing the effects of dark energy into focus. Dark energy is thought to be responsible for the expansion of our universe, and while the force itself remains ellusive, astronomers can track it by analyzing the rates at which other celestial objects appear to be moving away from us.

Data from the first three years of DESI’s survey—combined with observations of supernovae and the pervasive radiation leftover from the Big Bang—have hinted that dark energy may not be a constant force but is gradually weakening over time. An analysis of the full five years of data is scheduled to be released in 2027, which will scientists believe will paint a picture of the past and present of the universe more vividly than ever before.

Going forward, DESI’s observations will also serve as a reference and comparison point for other cosmic projects, such as NASA’s recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Researchers also plan to train artificial intelligence tools to accelerate analysis of the petabyte-scale astronomical data—within which much remains to be discovered.

“Explorations of our universe always start with images of the night sky,” said Arjun Day, co-director of Legacy Surveys and an astronomer with the National Science Foundation. “These data are fundamental to the investigation of the expansion history of the universe and the formation of our galaxy. But the skies belong to everyone, and this survey gives everyone the chance to marvel at their wonders.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

entries.title: Every Samsung Galaxy Phone Comes With This Unique Add-On
entries.summary: It’s called the Edge Panel. Here’s how to make the most of it.
entries.content:
If you opt for an Android phone over an iPhone, there are certain features you get as standard as part of Android. Then there are other features specific to certain manufacturers, as each Android phone maker puts its own spin on the software.

Pixel phones, for example, get the Now Playing widget on the home screen and lock screen that works like an instant Shazam. It'll tell you the name of the song playing in your environment before you've even searched for it.

With Samsung phones, one of the best perks isn't as widely known about or used as it should be. It's called the Edge Panel, and it works like a customizable shortcut bar that gives you speedy access to the other parts of your phone.

If you own a Galaxy device and have never come across the Edge Panel, or you used it once but have since forgotten about it, here's what it's capable of now—and how you can make the most of it to optimize your mobile experience.

How the Edge Panel Works

You can think of the Edge Panel as being a little bit like the Start menu on Windows, or the dock on macOS. It provides something that Android doesn't have by default, which is a user-configurable launcher for collecting your favorite apps and feature shortcuts.

When it's enabled, the Edge Panel appears as a faint line along the side of the screen, and you can swipe across it to open the pane. If you don't see it, head to Settings and choose Display > Edge Panels to turn it on (via the toggle switch) or customize what the panels show (by tapping the menu entry).

There are actually seven different types of panel to choose from, as you'll see when you start to customize the feature: Apps, People, Tasks, Weather, Tools, Clipboard, and Reminder. You can have just one of them active, or all seven, or something in between (once you've got the Edge Panel up, swipe across it to switch between the different types).

The names of these panels give you some idea of what they can do. You can use the Apps panel to access the apps you use the most, without having to hunt for them in the main app drawer or having them clutter up your home screen. You can also jump to your most important people on the Contacts panel in the same way.

The Clipboard panel gives you quick access to the phone clipboard, while Tasks features shortcuts such as taking screenshots, adding new calendar events, adding alarms, and taking a screenshot. Having these shortcuts on the Edge Panel means you don't have to dig through menus or remember key combinations for the same functions.

Tools is actually just a single tool: a compass that tells you your current location and points you north, south, east, or west. Weather is pretty self-explanatory, while Reminder syncs information from the Reminder app that comes preinstalled on Galaxy devices.

Customize the Edge Panel

The Edge Panel works fine in its default state, but to make the most of it you really need to set it up to suit you and the way you use your phone. From the main Settings menu, choose Display, then tap Edge Panels.

First, select Panels to pick which panes are shown. Put a check next to the panes you want to have available. If you tap the three dots (top right) then Reorder, you're able to choose the order they appear in as well—place the panes you use most often furthest to the left, as they'll be available in fewer swipes.

You can also tap the three dots then Hide on Lock screen if you don't want the Edge Panel to appear before you've unlocked your phone. Bear in mind that you might not want some information—such as the contents of the clipboard or your reminders—being available to anyone who picks up your handset.

With Apps, People, and Tasks, you can customize what's included. Just tap the Edit button underneath the pane. In each case, there are more available options than there are slots on the Edge Panel, so you need to prioritize accordingly.

Back on the Edge Panels screen, there are a couple of other options worth knowing about. If you pick Handle, you can set the properties of the little onscreen strip that Edge Panel is activated through. Pick the size and transparency level of the handle, its color, and which side of the screen it appears on.

Finally, there's the Show in landscape mode toggle switch; disable this if you don't want to see the Edge panel when you're using your phone in its landscape orientation. This mode is mainly used for watching videos and playing games, in which case the Edge Panel and its handle might distract you.

entries.title: Whispering Complaints Into Your Phone May Be the Future of Customer Feedback
entries.summary: Forget email surveys or long calls spent on hold. Voicebox lets people send customer feedback by recording a voice note on their phone.
entries.content:
Some of the hottest software this year revolves around capturing voices. Whether it’s the sharp dictations of Wispr or the always-listening ears of Granola, voice-centered software currently feels inescapable. Voice dictation is getting so sharp, in fact, that I often write drafts in my notepad and then dictate aloud to my laptop.

Some prognosticators have declared this to be a dramatic end-of-the-keyboard moment, where legions of white-collar workers will soon be quietly whispering into desk microphones rather than clacking away at keyboards. I disagree, but I do think these changes could upend how customers give feedback.

I rarely email customer support unless something substantially negative has happened and I’m fishing for a refund. I’m much more open to giving feedback by blabbering for 20 seconds into my phone, good or bad, than I am to waiting on hold for who knows how long until someone answers.

“In the last two years, we hit a tipping point,” says Karan Gupta, CEO of Voicebox, a startup designed to collect feedback via voice. “That voice could now be accurate. It could be fast.” His previous startup also relied on voice technology—an app called Alice designed for secure transcription.

Giving feedback through Voicebox is simple. Shoppers can scan a QR code or tap their phone to an NFC chip posted in a store and then say whatever they want. The feedback is automatically transcribed and sent to the company’s dashboard, with a sentiment analysis. Companies can also follow up over email, if needed. Voicebox has partnered with airport terminals so that travelers can give their two bits about bathroom messiness or gate directions.

Gupta wants this type of feedback to extend beyond corporate experiences. Earlier this year, Lena Dunham held an event in San Francisco for her book Famesick and flashed a Voicebox QR code on the screen. Numerous attendees gave feedback, sharing emotional messages about how they empathized with her medical journey. He sees this as an example of the public wanting to share more feedback more easily on topics they feel passionate about.

As part of this larger vision, Voicebox recently launched its “directory,” so feedback can be sent in from anywhere and, in future iterations, users can discover what other people are saying publicly about a specific business. I could give a quick opinion about my haircut on my way out of the barbershop by just whispering into my phone, or share advice for future visitors about navigating some hospital’s parking situation.

The directory expands Voicebox’s potential from a customer-complaint vehicle centered around business needs into something more like Google Maps, with crowd-spoken reviews. This voice-centric approach mirrors other popular software trends, where the future of dictation feels so natural that using your thumbs to tap away on a smartphone may feel cumbersome and outdated.

After chatting with Gupta, I opened the Voicebox directory and searched for, well, Voicebox. It was time for my voice to be heard. Though I’m still waiting for the couple sitting next to me at the airport to leave so I don’t feel awkward about whispering into my phone.

entries.title: How to Watch the Apple September Event (2026)
entries.summary: Apple’s annual hardware launch event may feel different as the company welcomes a new CEO alongside a folding iPhone.
entries.content:
Another Apple event is almost here, though this one will likely feel a little different than the September events of lore. It’s the first Apple event since CEO Tim Cook’s departure, and might be the first time the public gets a taste of how the company’s new CEO, John Ternus, can slip into those shoes.

The event will be livestreamed on September 9 at 10 am Pacific (1 pm Eastern). You can watch the stream right here on this page, or on Apple’s website and YouTube channel. Apple will also stream the event on its Apple TV devices and Apple TV+ streaming service. Leaks and rumors have left just about everyone expecting news about Pro-level iPhones and a long-awaited Apple foldable device.

Since the Covid pandemic, Apple has eschewed live presentations, instead inviting media and employees to the Apple campus to watch prerecorded videos of all its product announcements. WIRED will have reporters on the ground—you can follow along with all the action on our live blog, which will go live the morning of the event. WIRED will also have a roundup of everything the company announces for your perusal right after the event.

What to Expect

Thanks to leaks from sources like Bloomberg, the event is widely expected to be the moment Apple finally announces its long-rumored foldable iPhone. It’s bound to be pricey, with rumored estimates sitting around $2,000.

Apple is also expected to focus on premium products, chiefly the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12, and Apple Watch Ultra 4. That means Apple may push the launch of its base iPhone 18 to the spring of 2027. The move likely stems from increased manufacturing costs and limited product availability due to the ongoing memory crisis. It's also an effort to build hype for Apple’s more premium—and expensive—products, and maybe entice customers to sign up for the company’s new iPhone leasing program. We’ll likely see the mid-tier iPhone 18e at that spring event, alongside a second-gen iPhone Air.

New AirPods may also be on the table, though Apple’s heavily rumored AirPods Pro with cameras—designed to be the “eyes” of Siri for AI-powered visual assistance—could be delayed to later this year or to 2027.

If you’re hoping for new iPads, Macs, or home devices, well, you may have to wait a little longer. Apple announced a new Mac Mini and Mac Studio at the end of August, but the company may debut new home products, a new iPad Mini, and new MacBooks during events in October.

As for snagging devices right after Apple announces them this week, unconfirmed reports suggest the company will open iPhone preorders on September 12, a day later than it usually offers them, out of respect for the victims of 9/11. The following week is likely when the company will drop the final, official versions of its software, like iOS 27 and macOS 27.

entries.title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026 (So Far)?
entries.summary: I’ve tested every single Kindle. Here’s how Amazon’s ebook readers stack up.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There’s a lot to love about a Kindle if you’re a reader. If you’re looking for the best Kindle, you really can’t go wrong with any of the models. These Amazon-powered ebook readers let you bring thousands of books anywhere and typically give a month of battery life per charge. You can subscribe to get unlimited books from Amazon or get free books from your local library. Our guide will help you decode the differences to find which Kindle is right for you.

I've owned all kinds of Kindles, from the newest Kindle Scribes to hand-me-down base Kindles without a front light. The latter came from a friend who noticed I had spent my entire postpartum summer glued to library books on my phone, and I still have it to this day. But after trying all of the latest Kindles, I can say it's easy to spot the best one.

Read on to find out my favorite overall Kindle and my favorite Kindles for specific uses and younger readers. You can also check out my other buying guides made for readers like me, including the Best Kindle Accessories, Best E-Readers, Best Digital Notebooks, and Best Gifts for Book Lovers.

Updated September 2026: I've updated this guide with details about Amazon's price hike and which Kindles saw an increase (hint: It’s most of them).

Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

Model Display Resolution Color? Storage Weight Battery life Waterproof
Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 pixels per inch (ppi) No 16 GB 7.4 ounces Up to 12 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Scribe (2024, 2nd Gen) 10.2 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi No 16, 32, or 64 GB 15.3 ounces Up to 12 weeks No
Kindle Colorsoft (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (Black-and-White), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 7.6 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition (2024) 7 inches, adjustable warm light, auto-adjusting front light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 32 GB 7.7 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle Colorsoft Kids (2025) 7 inches, adjustable warm light 300 ppi (B&W), 150 ppi (Color) Yes 16 GB 11.8 ounces Up to 8 weeks Yes, IPX8
Kindle (2024, 11th Gen) 6 inches, adjustable front light 300 ppi No 16 GB 5.56 ounces Up to 6 weeks No

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only the recent Kindle Scribe models with the original price tag. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. It's interesting that none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it's also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including Signature versions:

  • Amazon Kindle (2024, 11th Gen): $150 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Gen): $200 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature (2024, 12th Gen): $250 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft: $290 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Signature: $320 (up $40)
  • Amazon Kindle Kids (2024, 2nd Gen): $180 (up $50)
  • Amazon Kindle Colorsoft Kids: $300 (up $30)

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I'd wait until Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday to shop when they're on sale. It's likely the sale prices will only bring the Kindle down to be the price it was before, but better than paying more.

What About the New Kindle Scribes?

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There's now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light. Like the second-generation model, they're a great choice for note-takers and students, especially with the long battery life, but I still prefer the second-generation's price point.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, slightly slimmer form factor, and updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you're reading without giving spoilers, though those won't arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can't do.

Overall, I'd say they're good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it's the better buy. It has some AI capabilities, but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design the new ones have. Amazon said it'll get the same homepage this year, but I haven't seen it so far. I'm disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable's line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

Accessories for Easier Reading

If you've ever had a long reading session that gives you hand cramps, these accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

Cases and Covers

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you're frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren't padded for serious drops, but are some of the best Kindle cases I've found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don't forget that the Kids' editions come with cases, so if you're buying one of those, you won't need a case.

About Those Older Kindles

Amazon doesn't release new Kindles often—the company usually takes a few years between models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor's stock starts to dwindle. It's not that we don't recommend these per se, but I only suggest these if you can find them on sale for the right price. And don't buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you're paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one. With this model, Amazon doubled the storage to 16 gigabytes and upgraded the display to 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution (up from 167 PPI). It's tough to find, and I usually don't see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It's waterproof too. We like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 gigabytes of storage. Don't recommend spending more than $100 if you can find them.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It's only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for under $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it's only available secondhand means you'll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, don't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn't spend more than $110 on this one.

FAQs

Which Kindle Models Lost Amazon Support and Kindle Store Access?

As of May 20, 2026, Amazon stopped supporting Kindles released in 2012 or earlier. That means these models will not be able to get new books through Amazon's services or be registered to an Amazon account. You will be able to read books already on the device, though, and can manually download documents and books via USB cable and via software like Calibre.

The following Kindle devices are impacted:

  • Kindle 1st Generation
  • Kindle 2nd Generation
  • Kindle DX
  • Kindle DX Graphite
  • Kindle Keyboard (3rd Generation)
  • Kindle 4
  • Kindle Touch
  • Kindle 5
  • Kindle Paperwhite 1st Generation

What’s the Best Way to Buy or Sell an Older Kindle?

Have an old Kindle lying around? Are you looking at a used one for sale? If you're trying to figure out what model it is, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model.

Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It's best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you'll still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. These models include the Kindle 2nd Generation (International), Kindle DX International, Kindle DX Graphite, Kindle Keyboard, Kindle 4th Generation, and Kindle 5th Generation.

How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle?

If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but there are millions of titles there, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial.

If you already pay for a Prime account, you're eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. There are not as many options as with Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you'll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you'll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It's still something, and there are even a few magazines.

If you don't want another monthly subscription and don't want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can't read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways:

  • Get a library card for your local branch.
  • Check your branch's website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.
  • Download directly to your Kindle library. They'll automatically be removed when they're due back.

If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books can be loaned.

What Else Can a Kindle Do?

Kindles have helpful features you may want to take advantage of. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages.

Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it's not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable.

While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type—there's even a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu too.

When a Kindle is connected to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you've pressed. It will also read a book aloud, though it doesn't sound nearly as nice as an audiobook.

Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you've read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads.

There's a web browser too if you're connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It's not the best, so I'd reserve it for emergency searches.

How Do You Update a Kindle?

When Amazon releases a new software update, it will download and install to your Kindle automatically when it's connected to Wi-Fi. You can check if you're on the latest software by going to Settings > Device Options > Advanced Options > Update Your Kindle. If it's not on the latest software version, you'll see an update available and the Kindle will then prompt you to download and install it.

What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar?

Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft.

Is This a Good Time to Buy a Kindle?

The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday, because Amazon often has steep discounts. Amazon has always had sales on some (if not all) of its Kindles on past Amazon Prime Day and similar events, like Amazon Big Deal Days.

You can also wait for other sale events if you're not ready to shop yet. Kindles are often on sale for Black Friday and Cyber Monday, which will occur in late November. Other sales often happen from time to time, but these sale events have consistent Kindle deals, so they're a good time to wait for if you want a better price.

Are Kindles Good for Students?

Kindles are great for students, though the model they'll like best will vary on how they use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, get a Kindle Scribe model. These models also have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. You can get some textbooks on a Kindle too, and send library books to them. For students who love to read but don't want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will be best for them.

entries.title: The Best Labor Day Mattress Deals on Beds We’ve Tried in Our Homes
entries.summary: It’s one of the best times of the year to buy a mattress, and our top tested picks are on sale.
entries.content:
Mattress deals come around pretty frequently, which means you can almost always save at least some money. But the very best deals come around Memorial Day, Labor Day, Black Friday, and Cyber Monday. If you're in the market for a new bed, or you need some sleep accessories like bedding, pillows, or blankets, we've found deals on tried-and-tested favorites.

Be sure to check out our related roundups for deals on tools, outdoor gear, tech, and kitchen goods.

Updated September 7: We've added new deals from Naturepedic, Birch, Bryte, Casper, and Purple, and ensured accuracy throughout.

WIRED Featured Mattress Deals

Labor Day Mattress Deals

Use code LUXE25 at checkout to save on the best mattress we've ever tried. Out of the hundreds of options we tested, this strikes the best balance between features and price for most sleepers. Individually wrapped springs provide support and pressure relief, and six layers of cushioning mean it's cozy but not overly plush. Make sure you get deep-pocketed sheets to accommodate the 13-inch height.

The best hybrid mattress has a fabric cover that helps to wick away and disperse your body heat. If you're a hot sleeper, it can help alleviate your problems. And it can help with back pain as well, thanks to its different types of coils arranged into three strategic zones. The pillow top can make the mattress feel softer than you might expect, so keep that in mind when you're choosing between the three firmness levels.

The best mattress for side sleepers has been a personal favorite among WIRED reviewers. It offers enough support to keep side sleepers' spines aligned without pushing things out of whack. This bed is bouncy and temperature-neutral, though you can pay a bit more for a cooling pillowtop that will decrease the mattress's firmness.

This affordable mattress is even more accessibly priced for Labor Day. It's a little firm, but offers great contouring and pressure relief, and motion stays isolated. The bed also doesn't get too hot overnight. If you prefer a slightly softer bed, you might want to pair this one with a mattress topper.

We quite like this inexpensive mattress. It's literally cool to the touch and therefore ideal for hot sleepers. And while you might think of cooling beds as being more suited to summer, they can also be nice in winter, since they'll help prevent you from overheating under all those covers. It's available in three firmness levels—we think the softest would be too soft.

Our top firm pick for back pain is still fine for side sleepers. It's very firm, with five layers of foam and coils, so it might be a bit shocking at first. But the support will help prevent and possibly even alleviate sore spots and back pain, and it's a particularly good pick for couples where one person might crave additional support for their spine while sleeping. The phase change material helps keep you cool.

We quite like this organic mattress, particularly for couples due to its modular design that allows for different firmness levels on either side. If you like a soft bed and your partner likes a firm bed, this mattress might be the perfect solution. You can swap out the layers for free for 100 nights to get your firmness level perfectly dialed in.

Our favorite organic mattress overall has a plus pillow top and individually wrapped coils that provide excellent support to any style of sleeper that prefers a medium firmness level. It isn't too stiff or too soft. I don't love the lack of edge support, but I do love the organic wool, latex, and cotton construction.

This smart mattress has 100 adjustable firmness levels that you can tweak on your own or let the bed do it on its own when sensing too much pressure in a certain area. There are also a lot of features to help with sleep, from the mattress rocking you to sleep to silently waking you up in the morning. You can read more about it in our in-depth review.

The Casper Dream Hybrid Mattress is a great option if you know you want memory foam. It'll contour your body and feel softer and warmer than some other beds, but thanks to the hybrid design that has coils inside, this bed won't cause more trouble than it's worth. It isn't exactly cooling, but it doesn't run too warm, and it doesn't have too much motion transfer. Consider it the elevated version of your favorite memory foam bed.

Labor Day Bedding and Accessory Deals

These bamboo sheets are a must-have, per resident sheet expert Nena Farrell. They're silky, soft, and cozy, with a supremely comfortable and lightweight drape. They'll make you feel sleepy right away and get even softer over time. We also like the color selection.

This is my favorite down comforter. I keep it on my bed as soon as it starts getting a little chilly out. It's fluffy and lofty, but still well ventilated, and the construction of the baffle boxes and down-proof fabric means I'm never getting stabbed with a feather in my sleep. It feels very cloud-like and is available in three warmth levels.

Our favorite mattress topper is organic. It's made with cotton and latex, so it's soft but still slightly springy and supportive. It's nice and plush but won't turn your bed into something too squishy or cradling. While it doesn't have straps, it's heavy enough to stay put.

Our favorite pillow is dense but adjustable, so you can make sure it cradles your head exactly how you want it to. This sale comes around relatively often but is still worth checking out, no matter how you like to sleep.

entries.title: Plastics Companies Are Writing Lesson Plans. What Could Go Wrong?
entries.summary: The science curriculum the industry is offering to schools casts plastics as safe, recyclable, and a source of good jobs. Critics say it’s propaganda.
entries.content:
This story originally appeared on Grist and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

This fall, 54 million K-12 students are headed back to the classroom for another year of lessons in all the classic subjects: math, English, history, biology. But there’s another subject that’s been sneaking into school curricula: plastics.

A new report from the nonprofit Plastic Pollution Coalition documents the many ways the plastics industry has been inserting its agenda into classrooms across the US—including through lesson plans and worksheets, hands-on science experiments, and a program called “PlastiVan” that travels from city to city teaching students about “the contribution plastics make to modern life.”

Industry interests offer these resources to teachers for free or for cheap, according to the report. The materials tend to highlight the necessity of plastics while downplaying their significant downsides to human health and the environment.

“When that information is provided to kids, it obfuscates the true impacts of plastic pollution,” said Madison Dennis, senior policy and advocacy manager for Plastic Pollution Coalition and one of the report’s main authors. Besides harming marine life, plastics can expose people to hazardous chemicals, clog storm drains and contribute to flooding, and release planet-warming greenhouse gases. The Plastic Pollution Coalition is calling for stricter school policies against the use of industry-sponsored learning materials.

The report lays out four case studies of plastics industry “propaganda” for schoolkids. One involves the Society of Plastics Engineers, or SPE, a trade group that recently became a division of the Plastics Industry Association. SPE’s lesson plans include activities like a “plastic scavenger hunt,” which aims for students to “understand that plastics are ubiquitous and their importance to society and their personal life.” A video titled “Your Bottle Means Jobs” explains how plastics recycling supports local employment.

Another case study highlights the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, an initiative of the Dow Chemical Company. One of the association’s lesson plans teaches elementary and middle school students how to compare the strength of various types of plastic bags that can be found in a grocery store. After a brief experiment, the lesson invites them to “pretend [they] are an employee for Dow Chemical Company” and are designing a plastic bag for a customer.

While many of the materials claim to support STEM learning objectives, they do so while promoting familiar industry talking points, emphasizing the affordability and safety of plastics. Some acknowledge plastic pollution as a serious problem, but they blame irresponsible consumer behaviors and, instead of recommending less plastic be produced, propose more recycling as the primary way to address it.

In reality, only 9 percent of all plastics are recycled worldwide, and scientists have repeatedly warned that recycling will be unable to keep up with projected growth in plastic production. Investigative reporting has shown that industry groups knew this decades ago, but promoted recycling anyway in order to defuse growing concern over plastic pollution.

Wendy Johnson, a science education specialist at the National Center for Science Education, said the industry’s lesson plans and worksheets don’t reflect good pedagogy. Materials claiming to be aligned with state-level STEM standards don’t say which standards they support, or how they’re aligned. Lesson plans instruct students to read teachers’ notes, or list industry-specific vocab terms like “stretch blow molding” or “thermosetting.”

“By using all of these technical terms, it’s tricking people into thinking … that they’re doing science,” Johnson told Grist. What the materials really teach, she said, is “ideological perspectives about the economy,” like the desirability of cheap consumer goods.

“It’s so clear that the purpose isn’t to make really clear, easy-to-use materials,” Johnson added. “The idea isn’t to teach,” but to get industry talking points into classrooms. The report documents plastics propaganda finding its way into schools since at least the 2000s. Between 2009 and 2011, for example, a plastics trade group lobbied the California Department of Education to add a section on “The Advantages of Shopping Bags” to the state’s high school textbooks. The PlastiVan initiative has been ongoing since 2011, and SPE claims it’s reached over 132,000 students in total.

Plastic Pollution Coalition suggests that the problem is particularly significant in schools located near petrochemical facilities. In Beaver County, Pennsylvania, for example, Shell operates a 386-acre plastics production complex and has invested millions of dollars in the development of plastics-related curricula and recycling programs, both for grade schoolers and for community college students. It has also donated hundreds of backpacks filled with school supplies, and bought one school a basketball court—seemingly in exchange for incorporating plastics recycling into the curriculum.

Shell didn’t respond to Grist’s request for comment. Neither did SPE, the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, nor the school district in Beaver County.

The report hints at a broader problem with STEM education in US public schools. Teachers often lack the time and money needed to design their own curricula, or to buy high-quality materials and lesson plans needed for in-class labs or science projects. When vested interests come along offering support—whether it’s the tobacco industry, the junk food industry, the pesticide industry, or the fossil fuel industry—it can be hard to say no.

“As a teacher, I’m always looking for free stuff,” said Suzie Hicks, a K-8 environmental educator in California who consulted on the Plastic Pollution Coalition report. Hicks said their education and background make them comfortable vetting materials for greenwashing—but that’s likely not the case with most teachers.

Dennis recommended that school boards adopt policies banning educational materials sponsored by the chemical, fossil fuel, and plastics industries. She also emphasized the need for better school funding more generally, so that teachers and districts aren’t so desperate for ready-made learning materials.

One way to achieve this would be to eliminate tax breaks for petrochemical processing and plastics production facilities, which deprive communities of much-needed cash.

Katie Allen, executive director of Algalita, a California-based environmental nonprofit that develops educational materials on plastic pollution, pushed back against the idea that schools should ban all industry-sponsored content.

“Once you start banning one thing, where does it end? What I want to do is give educators the benefit of the doubt and allow them to make their own decisions,” she told Grist. She argued that teachers should be trusted to properly contextualize industry materials—and that they could even use them to teach critical-thinking skills.

That said, there are plenty of educational materials on plastics that are developed by nonindustry sources. Algalita, for instance, offers free lesson plans on topics like plastic garbage patches in the oceans and biomagnification—the phenomenon where plastics build up inside sea creatures as you move up the food chain. The Story of Stuff, another nonprofit, offers a broader high school curriculum focused on the costs and consequences of producing consumer goods—including those made from plastics.

Those learning materials still come from organizations with an agenda. But Hicks argued they’re more trustworthy, since nonprofits usually aren’t trying to sell something.

Another option is for teachers to simply design their own curricula. That’s what Jacqueline Omania, a recently retired elementary school teacher in Berkeley, California, did in 2015. She turned her classroom into a zero-waste laboratory, and each year for 11 years, Omania and her students developed a set of zero-waste classroom agreements, vowing to minimize their plastics use—by swapping individual glue sticks for a communal tub of glue, for example—while also advocating for more systemic change, like by campaigning for a policy requiring Berkeley restaurants to stop giving out single-use plastic foodware.

“There are so many challenges in the world, but plastic is something tangible,” Omania said. “It’s right there in front of them, and they can see the difference that they’re actually making through their actions.”

entries.title: The Best Laptop Backpacks for Work, Travel, and Everything Between (2026)
entries.summary: The wrong bag can aggravate you every single day. These WIRED-tested picks get comfort, capacity, and organization just right.
entries.content:
Though I’ve been working from home for the past 15 years, both freelance and full-time, this often means needing to be available 24/7, so I typically carry my laptop everywhere I go—including sports practices, day trips, and vacations.

I have used many laptop backpacks in this time, and the dividing line between a work backpack that’s comfortable and fits seamlessly into your daily routine and one that’s aggravating at every turn is a fine one. If you’ve got limited closet space, it also helps if the backpack can pull double duty and be used for travel and/or hiking. The backpacks below are ones either I or another WIRED reviewer have used extensively in real life, taking on planes, hiking trails, vacations, and work trips.

For more bag and backpack recommendations, Bag Check features WIRED staffers’ favorite totes, sleeves, and packs. For more portable gear, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Chargers, Best Bluetooth Trackers, and Best Travel Adapters.

Updated September 2026: I've added the Paramount Daypack Lite 20L and the Navigator Backpack to my main picks. I've also included the Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack, North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro, Bagsmart Moss Backpack, Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack, and GoRuck G1 to our honorable mentions list.

Featured Products

Best Laptop Bag

I took this backpack on a weeklong work trip, where I bitched about it endlessly to everyone who would listen. However, I must fairly and objectively conclude that this bag offers tremendous value for the money. It's a light, attractive, rucksack-style backpack that's sleek and understated enough for work, and it's under $120. The 27-liter capacity accommodated enough gear for a full day's worth of travel, from a scarf for the plane to a water bottle, snacks, and other in-flight accouterments. It has a slim profile and lies close to your back, so it's not hard to carry and won't swing into people on the subway. The pockets are very minimal—just an exterior laptop pocket, an interior tablet sleeve, an interior zip pocket, and two large catch-all pockets—but they work if you already put your belongings in pouches anyway.

Certain design elements just felt cheap. I didn't like the curved zipper that gives you access to the main compartment—zippers that don't run straight are doomed to get stuck. One of the catch-all pockets is annoyingly located on the cover flap, where anything inside will flap and bang around. The luggage pass-through is a bare piece of webbing. However, it all works: it's light, affordable, and looks nice. The fabric is also water-resistant, so you can wear it in the rain! For most people, that's all that really matters. —Adrienne So

Capacity 27 liters
Weight Not stated
Materials 100 percent recycled plastic
Laptop size Can fit a 15-inch laptop
Warranty None; 30-day returns

Best Laptop Bag for Commuting

Thule's newest addition to its already solid backpack lineup was made specifically for schlepping gear to and from work on a daily basis, and it shows. The silhouette is sleek and aerodynamic, making it suitable for bike commuting (there's even a loop on the front to attach a bike light), and it's just big enough for a laptop, several notebooks, and maybe a jacket without feeling too big or bulky. The water bottle holder on the side is stretchy for a variety of sizes.

I also love the amount of organization inside for smaller things like pens and notebooks (the flap folds down for access to the interior, too, so you can access these things next to your desk), as well as the hidden yet easily accessible small pocket under the flap for wallet, keys, and phone. It's not the roomiest pack, so you're not carrying gym gear in this or taking it on an overnight trip, but if you're just going to and from the office with basics and a laptop, this is the most well-engineered option I've tried.

Capacity 20 liters
Weight Not stated
Materials Weather-resistant nylon
Laptop size Can fit a 16-inch laptop
Warranty Limited lifetime

Best Laptop Bag for Travel

Aer has a lock on the tech-minimalist aesthetic with its no-frills, black Cordura bags; this is the larger version of the popular City Pack. Though there is a newer version of the Travel Pack—the Travel Pack 4 is supposedly more streamlined—my husband and I have both been using this bag constantly for two years and have zero complaints, which is rare. It's also still in pristine condition, despite going on at least 10 work trips between the two of us.

Any backpack need you might have, the Travel Pack can probably cover it, from hiking to one-bag travel. The front zip pocket has built-in organization for all your pens, cords, and notebooks, and the main compartment opens clamshell-style for packing cubes or gym gear. It covers all the bases without feeling too fiddly. However, note it's not the lightest pack and would likely be frustratingly bulky for commuters.

Capacity 35 liters
Weight 4.12 lbs
Materials 1680-denier Cordura ballistic nylon
Laptop size Can fit a 16-inch laptop
Warranty Lifetime

Best Minimalist Laptop Bag

I have never received as many approving comments on a backpack as I have when I tested this one on a three-day work trip (I was told by three people in a day that I sold them on it). It's a good-looking, structured bag with vegan leather accents and gigantic padded back panels and padded shoulder straps. There are little details like vegan leather pull tabs on the interior pockets, so you're not fumbling around for the pocket opening (I have never had this problem, but you do you). The fabric is also waterproof, and you can buy optional accessories like a rain cover.

I really liked the interior organization—for example, the padded, suspended tech pocket has two pockets, one for your laptop and one for your iPad or Kindle. However, all those padded panels and good-looking accents come at a price—this bag is disproportionately heavy. I couldn't go on a 20-minute bike ride without stopping to give my shoulders a break. Other details seem like they were designed by aliens who had never seen backpacks before. My tiny 18-ounce Owala tips right out of the water bottle pocket because its lip slants forward. The capacity is surprisingly small for how bulky it is, and a 100-percent plastic backpack just should not cost $249. However, everyone else loves this backpack, so here it is. —Adrienne So

Capacity 22 liters
Weight 2.69 lbs
Materials 100 percent recycled polyester with plastic accents
Laptop size Can fit a 17-inch laptop
Warranty 5 years

Best Trendy Laptop Bag

Given that Comfrt is primarily known for its viral “airplane mode” hoodies, I was impressed with this au courant puffy backpack’s finish and construction for the price. (Though note there's no warranty, just a 30-day return policy.) My teen son has been testing it now for about three weeks, packing it to the gills and throwing it into his locker and on the ground for after-school sports. Though it looks like it might be fragile, the water-resistant polyester exterior still has nary a scratch or tear.

The straps are well-padded, the laptop compartment in the back is lined with a minky fabric, and there's a hidden pocket for valuables. It's also got a luggage pass-through and two generously sized pockets on either side for water bottles or whatever else (my son keeps a Shark ChillPill in one). Best yet, this pack fits far more than it seems like it will at 25 liters—more than some of the similar-sized backpacks on this list. It's perfect for high school or college students who need to pack in textbooks as well as incidentals and gym clothes. Color options include black (shown), navy, espresso, and pink.

Capacity 25 liters
Weight Not stated
Materials Polyester
Laptop size Can fit a 16-inch laptop
Warranty None; 30 days

Best Camera Bag

Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. It's a 2025 update to Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronouned "provoke") line, adding zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. Julian likes that it never feels cramped like other camera bags.

He also recommends pairing it with Wandrd's Essential Camera Cube (Photo Bundle) to get the most out of it. The straps and back are well padded, and he's been comfortable carrying it for hours.

Best Laptop Bag for Organization

The pockets on the front of this burly, workhorse are so versatile and accessible—five exterior organizational pockets, where most backpacks have one or two. You can access the laptop pocket from either the interior of the backpack or the side. There are internal compression straps, so you can tie things down or organize them inside the bag. It's made from PFC-free, Bluesign-certified, recycled, high-denier ballistic nylon. There are lots of thoughtful design details; for example, the water bottle pocket is in the center of the bag, and not the side, so carrying a full water bottle doesn't give you scoliosis after a long day. The zippers are YKK coil zippers, instead of toothed ones, so they don't get stuck or tear at your knuckles if you drag them against the zipper while rummaging around.

I have two complaints, which is that the backpack itself is slightly too tall for the luggage pass-through to work with my carry-on. The handle doesn't extend all the way through the pass-through. Also, all this hardware and sewing comes at a price. It is heavy, and it's expensive. But it will last you forever. I have this pink one, and my spouse has a 10-year-old black Synik 22 that still looks brand-new. —Adrienne So

Capacity 26 liters
Weight 2 lbs, 11 oz
Materials 620D ballistic nylon exterior, 210D nylon ripstop interior
Laptop size Can fit a 14–15-inch laptop
Warranty Lifetime

Retrofit an Existing Backpack

WIRED's laptop expert, Luke Larsen, swears by this padded laptop sleeve if you don't need a full backpack or just want to add a bit more padding to your laptop (or multiple laptops). It's got plenty of room for accessories like a keyboard or laptop stand, and he was able to fit a power adapter and cable. He was able to barely fit the 16-inch size inside his Herschel laptop bag, but if you have a smaller laptop, the 14-inch size may be a better universal fit for most bags.

Capacity n/a (11 × 14.6 × 1 in for the 16-inch size)
Weight 13.4 ounces
Materials Recycled polyester and nylon
Laptop size Can fit a 14- or 16-inch laptop
Warranty 3 years

More Laptop Bags We Like

Eagle Creek Tour Lite Travel Pack for $159: This rugged yet lightweight pack features a lifetime warranty, a generously sized water bottle holder, a strap for carrying it horizontally, and one roomy clamshell-style compartment with compression straps. The laptop compartment is divided and well padded, and the beefy straps make the whole thing feel comfortable and well balanced. There just isn't enough organization to make it practical for work.

The North Face Base Camp Voyager Pro Travel Pack for $203: As an unrepentant overpacker, I love the modular system this bag is a part of—you can attach the either the smaller 15-liter Voyager Pro Lightweight Pack ($80) or Voyager Pro Crossbody ($75) to the front via clips and MOLL-E webbing, and the Base Camp Voyager Travel Pouch ($30) to one of the front straps for easy access to phone, keys, and passport. I carried both configurations around a weekend-long soccer tournament and felt like a decorator crab. (In the best way.) I did, however, find the larger and smaller backpacks a bit too big and small, respectively, for work, and the fabric to be a bit stiff and unyielding for daily use—it's likely best kept to outdoor pursuits.

Bagsmart Moss Backpack for $90: Another thoughtfully designed pack from Bagsmart, with the softest, minkiest laptop compartment of any pack I tested. It's on the smaller side, but I carried it for 4 miles full of groceries and felt nary a pinch or strain. The only issue I had was with the appearance—I thought it looked like something a college-aged girl would carry, but partway into my test period someone asked me if it was a little kids’ backpack, and now I can't unsee it.

The Brown Buffalo Conceal Pack for $239: Streamlined and sleek with a Cordura exterior, this bag features two pockets lined with a Velcro-type material to which you can affix organizers (not included), or you can slip a laptop into either one. I used this pack to commute to and from the hospital where my husband was having surgery, and because there's no smaller zip pouch, I wished I had one of the “Mods" to hold my phone and keys. I also had mixed feelings about the water bottle holder being inside the backpack, though it does make for a less lopsided carry.

GoRuck G1 for $395: This is WIRED operations manager Scott Gilbertson's do-anything, go-anywhere bag. He says it's the best backpack he's ever used and has been a trusty and versatile companion for the past three years. While it's made specifically for rucking, it's also got a laptop compartment, so you can tote your computer while you're marching up hills with other heavy things.

Janji Revy Pack for $198: I was going to include this as my best running backpack, since one way you can sneak exercise into your day is if you run to and fro from your home to your workplace, kids' school, or coffee shop. However, this backpack sold out before I could write about it, so the hunt continues. —Adrienne So

Away Commuter Backpack for $182: We very much like everything Away makes, from carry-on luggage to toiletry bags. This bag is attractive, water-resistant, and full of organized pockets; the hardware also feels premium. But $225 is steep, and we have other options with similar functionality for cheaper. —Adrienne So

Cotopaxi Allpa Travel Pack Del Dìa for $230: WIRED senior innovation writer Jeremy White loves Cotopaxi's Allpa Travel Pack so much he wrote an entire paean to it, praising the ethical manufacturing practices and ability to fill it with packing cubes. (It's also got a padded laptop slot.)

Able Carry Daily Backpack for $139: This pack is thin, so you can stuff it to the brim before it starts to get bulky. And stuff it full you can, because it has a pocket for everything. The Thirteen Daybag for $158 is similar but slightly smaller. —Adrienne So

Laptop Bags to Avoid

Mission Workshop Rhake for $435: This roll-top bag has a ton of pockets, and its two-layer weatherproof construction and Velcro closures keep the contents dry. But those pockets aren't easy or fast to access, it's heavy, and it's even pricier than when we first tried it (and rising). —Adrienne So

Adventurist Classic Backpack for $65: This affordable, attractive backpack rings in at well under $100, and for every backpack purchased, 25 meals are donated to families across the United States. It's pretty much just a leather pouch that you wear on your back; however, the showy leather straps were annoying and useless. —Adrienne So

entries.title: Create Custom Windows 11 Notifications to Remind Yourself of Anything
entries.summary: Take full control of your desktop alerts by sending yourself recurring reminders and custom notifications triggered by specific events.
entries.content:
While there are plenty of ways to limit notifications on our digital devices and avoid distraction overload, there’s nothing inherently wrong with these alerts. They just need to be well managed and kept in their place.

Keeping notifications useful and timely can help you get more done in the day, not less, and Windows 11 comes with built-in tools for setting up custom notifications that run on a schedule you specify.

You can use these scheduled notifications however you want. Maybe you need reminders to take breaks, or you want to make sure you devote specific blocks of time to certain projects, or you need alerts for when it’s time to go and pick the kids up.

However you want to use these custom notifications, here’s how to set them up—plus some extra apps that can help too.

Custom Notifications in Windows 11

If you want to set up custom notifications in Windows 11 without turning to an app, the Task Scheduler is the utility you want. Type “task scheduler” into the search box on the taskbar or the Start menu, then select it when it appears.

Open the Action menu, choose Create Basic Task, and then give it a suitable name and description so you can identify it later. Click Next, and you can set the frequency of the notification: Your options are Daily, Weekly, Monthly, One time, When the computer starts, When I log on, and When a specific event is logged, so there’s a lot of flexibility.

Click Next again, and if you’ve chosen a recurring task then you can set exactly when it recurs—4 pm every afternoon, for example. Click Next, then choose Start a program, and select Next again. This opens up the dialog box screen for composing your notification.

In the Program/script field, you need to enter “msg,” and in the Add arguments (optional) field, you put your actual notification text: “Reminder: get up and do some stretching” or whatever it happens to be. With another click on Next you can review your notification, and then choose Finish to confirm.

Your notification is created, and will pop up at the specified time, whether or not Task Scheduler is open. If you ever need to edit or delete the task, you can head back to Task Scheduler to find it—it’ll be listed under the Task Scheduler Library heading, and you can right-click on the task to make changes.

Setting Notifications Through Apps

The appeal of the Task Scheduler is that it’s built right into the Windows operating system, so you don’t need any other apps running to get your notifications, but there are ways to do this with apps as well. The Microsoft Clock app comes preinstalled with Windows, for example, and lets you set custom alarms.

Once you’ve launched the app through the Start menu or taskbar search box, select Alarm to set one. Click on the + (plus) button in the lower right corner to create a new alarm, and you can give it a name—which is essentially the text you want for your notification. You can configure the time for the alarm, and when it should recur.

If that doesn’t do exactly what you want, another app that comes with Windows is Microsoft To Do—again, you can search for it from the taskbar or Start menu. As the name suggests, this is a fully fledged to-do app, but you can create custom notifications through it by attaching reminders to tasks.

Click Add a task to get started, and once you’ve given your new task a name, you can set the reminder details: What time and date you want the alert to appear, and whether or not you want the notification to repeat on a schedule. There's also the option to put your reminders into categories, if needed.

In terms of third-party apps, any clock, reminder, or to-do list app would do the job—something like TickTick, for instance—but these take you further away from the clean simplicity of just generating custom notifications and nothing else. Those apps will also come with extras you don’t necessarily need for this particular task.

entries.title: These Cyborg Cockroaches Could Save Your Life
entries.summary: The team embedded electrodes into live cockroaches, then outfitted them with cameras and injection devices to deliver medication via remote control.
entries.content:
Small robots and drones have increasingly been used to help respond to disasters, reaching locations that are too hard or too dangerous to send humans, such as collapsed buildings. Many of these efforts have been focused on search and rescue. But new research shows how bugs—with their ability to crawl through even narrower gaps in rubbled—outfitted with electrodes could be used as the next generation of first responders.

A research team from the University of Queensland (UQ) and the University of New South Wales (UNSW) have developed the “Paraborg” to not only help with searching for victims, but also administer first aid. While the idea of receiving medical care from a cockroach might be a little skin-crawling, the new cyborg bug could one day help buy human rescuers valuable time in a disaster zone.

“Cyborg insects have been designed for ‘search and explore’ missions for the past couple of decades,” Tan Vo Doan, a bio-robotics researcher at UQ, says in a press release. “We wanted to take the next step.”

The team relied on a giant burrowing cockroach that inhabits northern Queensland to develop the Paraborg, which they documented in a recent paper published the journal Advanced Science. The armored cockroach is up to 87 millimeters (3.5 inches) in length and weighs up to 40 grams (1.4 ounces).

Taking advantage of this large size, the research team developed two types of Paraborgs with different functions: one equipped with a camera to film the condition of disaster victims, and another with an automatic injection mechanism to administer medication. Cockroaches can carry up to 1.5 times its body weight. In practice, a cockroach equipped with the injection mechanism saw its total height increase by about 15 millimeters and its weight by about 17 grams, which the study found did not significantly impair its normal movements. To create the cyborg cockroaches, the team anesthetized them when the electrodes and microchips were attached, and they lived as normal cockroaches once the equipment was removed.

By applying electrical stimuli to electrodes embedded in the cockroach’s antennae and cerci—a pair of protruding sensory organs at the rear of the abdomen—researchers were able to remotely control the bug’s direction of travel and walking speed.

They were able to steer the roach by stimulating each antenna independently, while stimulating both cerci controlled the pace. The scientists administered different frequencies between 10 and 40 hertz after finding that anything over 50 hertz became ineffective over time.

The injection mechanism is a small device that deploys a syringe using a spring system. That triggers a process that breaks the seal between a chamber containing citric acid and another containing baking soda. The resulting chemical reaction—basically the same one you might’ve done as a kid to make a volcano with baking soda and vinegar—creates enough carbon dioxide to push the plunger on the syringe and administer medication.

For the study, the research team remotely controlled a cockroach to travel from its starting point through three checkpoints and administer an injection to a simulated target.

The results showed that the success rate for injections made at close range—within 150 millimeters of the target—topped out at approximately 95 percent. The success rate for the entire sequence of tasks—from departure to completion of the injection—was 72 percent.

The researchers also successfully demonstrated teamwork, where one cockroach uses a camera to locate a simulated target while another serves as the injector.

Although the research team has previously developed cyborg beetles capable of climbing vertical walls, they note that larger cockroaches are better-suited for carrying specialized rescue and medical equipment.

While the results of the new research are promising, the experiment didn’t replicate the complex environmental conditions found at actual disaster sites, such as debris, uneven terrain, and shifting landscapes.

Vo Doan expressed hope that, if resources can be secured to speed up research and field testing, a rescue team of cyborg insects could be deployed at actual disaster sites within five to 10 years.

“Rather than building one robot to do everything, we can harness the natural strengths of different insects and equip them for different missions,” Vo-Doan says.

This story was originally published in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.
